title: Tensor-Product Crystals and Highest-Weight Crystal Uniqueness

items.title: Tensor products of integrable weight modules and of their crystal lattices
items.statement:
Let $M_1,M_2$ be chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $M_1\otimes M_2$ carry the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module structure of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] given by the coproduct $\Delta E_i=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i$, $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$, $\Delta K_h=K_h\otimes K_h$ of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. Then:

(a) **Grading.** $M_1\otimes M_2$ is a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module for $(M_1\otimes M_2)_\mu=\bigoplus_{\mu_1+\mu_2=\mu}(M_1)_{\mu_1}\otimes(M_2)_{\mu_2}$, a direct sum by [[thm-tensor-products-commute-with-arbitrary-direct-sums]].

(b) **Integrability.** If $M_1,M_2$ are integrable then so is $M_1\otimes M_2$: $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every pure tensor, hence on the whole module.

(c) **Finite weights and bounded support.** If in addition every label-weight space of $M_1,M_2$ is finite dimensional and each weight set is contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$, then the same holds for $M_1\otimes M_2$.

(d) **Tensored lattices.** If $(L_1,B_1),(L_2,B_2)$ are crystal bases of $M_1,M_2$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]), then $L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2$ is a free $A_0$-submodule of $M_1\otimes M_2$ generating it over $\mathbb Q(q)$, satisfies $(L_1\otimes L_2)_\mu=\bigoplus_{\mu_1+\mu_2=\mu}(L_1)_{\mu_1}\otimes(L_2)_{\mu_2}$, and $B_1\otimes B_2$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $(L_1\otimes L_2)/q(L_1\otimes L_2)$ compatible with these weight decompositions.

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Use the balanced tensor universal property for the coproduct action and direct-sum compatibility for the label grading. Correct inverse-parameter Gaussian expansion and toral commutation prove local nilpotence of F; positive-parameter expansion proves it for E. Finite root-cone intervals prove finite label spaces under the additional hypotheses. Two free bases give the full tensor lattice, and explicit quotient inverses give the product residue basis. Only finite choice is needed.

items.title: The tensor product crystal $B_1\otimes B_2$ and its two-case convention
items.statement:
Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be crystals, meaning the data $(B,wt,\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i,\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i)$ attached to a crystal basis $(L,B)$ of an integrable module by [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]] and [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]: $wt:B\to P$ is the weight function, $\varepsilon_i(b)=\max\{n:\tilde e_i^nb\ne0\}$ and $\varphi_i(b)=\max\{n:\tilde f_i^nb\ne0\}$ are finite, $\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$, and $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ are the partial maps $B\to B\cup\{0\}$ of [[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]].

The **tensor product crystal** $B_1\otimes B_2$ is the following data on $B_1\times B_2$, whose elements are written $b_1\otimes b_2$:

(i) $wt(b_1\otimes b_2):=wt(b_1)+wt(b_2)$;

(ii) $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, and $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2)$;

(iii) $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, and $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=b_1\otimes\tilde e_ib_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2)$.

By convention a product is $0$ as soon as the operator applied to the selected factor is $0$; the **left factor is preferred** exactly in the displayed cases, so the assignment is left-to-right, matching the left-to-right order of the module tensor product $M_1\otimes M_2$ under the coproduct of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. The **equality case** $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ is split: $\tilde e_i$ acts on the first factor while $\tilde f_i$ acts on the second. The asymmetry is not free: with the same strict or non-strict comparison used for both operators the partial-inverse axiom fails, as the counterexample on the companion page records, while the displayed convention is internally consistent by the lemma on this page computing $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ of $B_1\otimes B_2$.

The functions $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ of $B_1\otimes B_2$ are read off from the two-case operators as maximal iterated powers, exactly as in [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]. This definition only fixes combinatorial data and asserts nothing about an arbitrary pair of crystals: it does not claim that every such datum arises from a module tensor product. When $B_1,B_2$ are the crystals of crystal bases of integrable modules, the tensor product theorem later on this page proves that $(L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2,\,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$ with these operators, and only through that theorem are the values finite and nonnegative a priori. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition fixing the data, the left-to-right preference and the equality cases; the two comparisons are those of JKK Theorem 5.2 (printed pp. 20-21). The asymmetry is forced: if $\tilde f_i$ used the non-strict comparison, then at a vertex with $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ it would act on the first factor, while at the image the resulting $\tilde e_i$ would act on the second, so $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i$ would fail to be the identity on existing edges; the companion-page counterexample exhibits this on $V(2)\otimes V(2)$ for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, and the lemma on this page verifies the displayed convention by a finite case check. The remaining content is bookkeeping: $(b_1,b_2)\mapsto b_1\otimes b_2$ is a bijection, weight additivity is declared, and no existence or axiom claim is made here. The comparison with the module tensor product and the identification of $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are the content of the two following items.

items.title: The $i$-string components of a lattice vector and the single surviving component modulo $q$
items.statement:
Let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of an integrable weight module $M$ in the sense of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]], let $i\in I$, $\lambda\in P$ and $u\in L_\lambda$, and let $u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n$ be the admissible $i$-string decomposition of $u$: the sum is finite, $u_n\in\ker E_i\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, and $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle h_i,\lambda+n\alpha_i\rangle$ ([[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]]). Then:

(a) **Components lie in the lattice.** $u_n\in L\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ for every $n$.

(b) **Lattice string decomposition.** $L_\lambda=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\tilde f_i^{\,n}\bigl(L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}\cap\ker E_i\bigr)$, the sum being direct because admissible decompositions are unique; equivalently $L=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\tilde f_i^{\,n}(L\cap\ker E_i)$.

(c) **Single surviving component.** If $u+qL=0$ in $L_\lambda/qL_\lambda$, then $u_n\in qL$ for every $n$. If $u+qL\in B_\lambda$, then there is exactly one index $n_0$ with $u_{n_0}\notin qL$, and for it $u_{n_0}+qL\in B_{\lambda+n_0\alpha_i}$, $u\equiv F_i^{(n_0)}u_{n_0}\pmod{qL}$ and $u_{n_0}+qL=\tilde e_i^{\,n_0}(u+qL)$; in particular $n_0=\varepsilon_i(u+qL)$ ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]), and $\tilde e_iu$ and $\tilde f_iu$ are the residues of $F_i^{(n_0-1)}u_{n_0}$ and $F_i^{(n_0+1)}u_{n_0}$.

Everything is a statement about the fixed lattice $L$ and the operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$; no finite-dimensionality, bounded support, uniform nilpotence or choice principle is assumed. Here $F_i^{(-1)}u$ is interpreted as $0$, and $F_i^{(a+1)}u=0$ for a top of coroot weight $a$, so the final formulas include both finite-string endpoints.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The tails $T_n=\tilde e_i^{\,n}u$ lie in $L\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, and $T_n=\sum_{k\ge n}F_i^{(k-n)}u_k$ with $\tilde f_iT_{n+1}=T_n-u_n$ for every $n\ge0$. Indeed $T_0=u\in L_\lambda$ and each $\tilde e_i$ preserves $L$ and raises the label weight by $\alpha_i$ by [F2], so $T_n\in L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ by [F1]; on the string decomposition $\tilde e_i$ substitutes $F_i^{(k)}u_k\mapsto F_i^{(k-1)}u_k$ by [F2], giving $T_n=\sum_{k\ge n}F_i^{(k-n)}u_k$, and applying $\tilde f_i$ to $T_{n+1}=\sum_{k\ge n+1}F_i^{(k-n-1)}u_k$ shifts every divided power up by one, so $\tilde f_iT_{n+1}=\sum_{k\ge n+1}F_i^{(k-n)}u_k=T_n-u_n$. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Every $u_n$ lies in $L$. For $n\ge0$ the identity $u_n=T_n-\tilde f_iT_{n+1}$ of step 1.1 exhibits $u_n$ as a difference of two elements of $L$: $T_n,T_{n+1}\in L$ by step 1.1 and $\tilde f_iL\subseteq L$ by [F1]; the weight of $u_n$ is $\lambda+n\alpha_i$ by the Given, so $u_n\in L\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}=L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$. This proves (a). [step 1.1, F1]

2.2 Residue components when $u\in qL$. Step 1.1 gives $u_n=\tilde e_i^{\,n}u-\tilde f_i\tilde e_i^{\,n+1}u$. Both operators preserve $L$ and are linear, hence preserve $qL$; therefore every $u_n$ lies in $qL$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 The lattice string decomposition (b). For a top $v\in L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}\cap\ker E_i$ the vector $\tilde f_i^{\,n}v$ equals $F_i^{(n)}v$ by [F2] applied to the one-term admissible decomposition of $v$, so $u=\sum_n\tilde f_i^{\,n}u_n$ with $u_n\in L\cap\ker E_i$ by step 2.1, and conversely every $\tilde f_i^{\,n}(L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}\cap\ker E_i)$ lies in $L$ by iterated stability [F1]. For a relation $\sum_n\tilde f_i^{\,n}v_n=0$ with $v_n\in L\cap\ker E_i$ first discard the top components of coroot weight $a<n$: their $n$-th lowering image is $F_i^{(n)}v_n=0$ by [F3]; the remaining representatives are admissible, so the relation is an admissible decomposition of $0$ and every remaining $v_n=0$ by the uniqueness half of [F3]. Hence the sum is direct and equals $L_\lambda=\bigoplus_\mu L_\mu$'s $\lambda$-part. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3]


3.2 Residue components when $u+qL=b\in B_\lambda$. Put $N:=\varepsilon_i(b)$. Reducing the identity of step 1.1 gives $u_n+qL=\tilde e_i^{\,n}b-\tilde f_i\tilde e_i^{\,n+1}b$. For $n<N$ the partial-inverse axiom gives $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i^{\,n+1}b=\tilde e_i^{\,n}b$, so this difference is zero. For $n=N$ it is $\tilde e_i^{\,N}b\in B$, and for $n>N$ both terms vanish. Thus exactly $u_N$ is outside $qL$, with residue $\tilde e_i^{\,N}b$. Since $F_i^{(n)}u_n=\tilde f_i^{\,n}u_n$ on a top component, all other summands lie in $qL$; consequently $u\equiv F_i^{(N)}u_N\pmod{qL}$. This proves (c), including $N=0$, where raising, rather than lowering, kills the top. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, F1, F2, F4]

4.1 The remaining residual formulas and the choice audit. By the previous steps, when $u+qL\in B_\lambda$ every component $u_n$ with $n\ne n_0$ lies in $qL$, so $\tilde e_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and $\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ are congruent modulo $qL$ to $F_i^{(n_0-1)}u_{n_0}$ and $F_i^{(n_0+1)}u_{n_0}$ respectively, with $F_i^{(-1)}u_0:=0$ when $n_0=0$ and $F_i^{(a+1)}u_n:=0$ beyond the string bottom by [F3]; this proves the final clause of (c). Every step used only the fixed lattice $L$, the finitely supported string decomposition of $u$ and the stated operators, so no finite-dimensionality, bounded support, uniform nilpotence or choice principle is assumed. [step 3.2, step 2.2, F1, F2, F3, given] ∎

items.title: Highest weight elements, lowering-generated sets and highest weight crystals
items.statement:
Let $B$ be a crystal, meaning the data $(B,wt,\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i,\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i)$ attached to a crystal basis or to a tensor product of such data ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]], [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]]).

A vertex $b\in B$ is a **highest weight element** (a highest vertex, a maximal vector) of weight $\lambda\in P$ if $wt(b)=\lambda$ and $\tilde e_ib=0$ for every $i\in I$. The **lowering-generated set** of $b$ is

$$F(b):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}b:\ r\ge0,\ i_1,\dots,i_r\in I\}\setminus\{0\},$$

the set of all nonzero iterated lowering images of $b$; it contains $b$ and is closed under nonzero images of every $\tilde f_i$. It need not be closed under raising: at the bottom $b$ of a two-vertex rank-one string, $F(b)=\{b\}$ while $\tilde e_i b$ is the top vertex. The **connected component** $C(b)$ of $b$ is the smallest subset of $B$ containing $b$ and closed under nonzero images of $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ for all $i$; by the partial-inverse axiom this is the connected component of the underlying coloured graph.

$B$ is a **highest weight crystal of highest weight $\lambda$** if $B$ has a highest weight element $b$ of weight $\lambda$ and $B=F(b)$.

The definition deliberately separates two conditions. Always $F(b)\subseteq C(b)$, and a highest vertex need not generate $B$: in a tensor product $B_1\otimes B_2$ a vertex with $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\varphi_i(b_1)$ for all $i$ is highest while $B_1\otimes B_2$ is in general larger than its lowering-generated set (the companion page computes both cases). Conversely, for abstract crystals the two conditions do not determine $B$ up to isomorphism: the source literature records that not every connected crystal with a highest weight element of weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $B(\lambda)$. In this library crystals come from crystal bases of modules, and uniqueness for those is a theorem proved later on this page, not a consequence of this definition.

For the canonical objects, $B(\lambda)=\mathcal B(\lambda)$ denotes the crystal of the simple highest weight module $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ ([[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]]) and $P^+$ the dominant integral labels ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); that $B(\lambda)$ is a highest weight crystal of highest weight $\lambda$ is the next theorem. The operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ used throughout are those of [[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]]. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition with the two conditions stated separately: $F(b)$ is the closure of $\{b\}$ under the lowering operators alone, while $C(b)$ is its closure under both, the usual graph component. The distinction is not cosmetic: the two-case rule shows that a highest vertex of a tensor product generates one $i$-string colour at a time, so $F(b)$ is usually strictly smaller than the crystal. The abstract-crystal caveat is recorded so that the definition is not read as a uniqueness assertion; components are identified only through the crystal-basis theorems later on this page. No objects are chosen and no basis is selected. The comparison with the canonical $B(\lambda)$ is deferred to the next theorem, which is the first place where existence of a highest weight crystal is asserted.

A connected crystal $B$ is a highest weight crystal with highest weight $\lambda$ if there exists a highest weight element $b_\lambda$ of weight $\lambda$ such that $B=F\{b_\lambda\}$', followed by 'Note not every highest weight crystal with highest weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $B(\lambda)$'.

items.title: The crystal basis of a tensor product and the two-case operator rule
items.statement:
Let $M_1,M_2$ be integrable chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules with crystal bases $(L_1,B_1)$, $(L_2,B_2)$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]), and let $M_1\otimes M_2$ be the integrable module of [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]].

Then $(L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2,\,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$, and its crystal is the tensor product crystal $B_1\otimes B_2$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]]: for all $b_1\in B_1$, $b_2\in B_2$ and $i\in I$,

$$\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}\qquad \tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde e_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}$$

with value $0$ as soon as the selected factor maps to $0$. In particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ map $B_1\otimes B_2$ into $(B_1\otimes B_2)\cup\{0\}$, and for all $b,b'\in B_1\otimes B_2$ one has $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$, so the partial-inverse axiom holds. The equality case $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ is resolved as in the definition: $\tilde f_i$ acts on the second factor and $\tilde e_i$ on the first.

No finite dimensionality, bounded support or uniform nilpotence is assumed, and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Reduction to single string components. Fix $b_1\otimes b_2\in B_1\otimes B_2$ and lifts $u_j\in L_j$ with $u_j+qL_j=b_j$, and put $n_j:=\varepsilon_i(b_j)$. By [F2] applied to $u_j$ there are top components $w_j\in L_j\cap\ker E_i$ with $w_j+qL_j=\tilde e_i^{\,n_j}b_j\in B_j$ and $u_j\equiv F_i^{(n_j)}w_j\pmod{qL_j}$; hence $u_1\otimes u_2\equiv h:=F_i^{(n_1)}w_1\otimes F_i^{(n_2)}w_2\pmod{q(L_1\otimes L_2)}$ (expand the difference as in the bilinearity of the tensor product), and $h+q(L_1\otimes L_2)=b_1\otimes b_2$ because the residue of $F_i^{(n_j)}w_j$ is $b_j$ by [F2]. [F2, given, algebra]

1.2 The rank-one block. The top $w_j$ lies in $\ker E_i\cap (L_j)_{\mu_j}$ with $a_j:=\langle h_i,\mu_j\rangle\ge0$ by [F5]; the divided powers $F_i^{(k)}w_j$, $0\le k\le a_j$, form the string basis of the finite-dimensional $U_i$-submodule $N_j:=U_iw_j$, all of them lie in $L_j$ by [F2], and on this string $\tilde f_i$ acts as the divided-power shift and $\tilde e_i$ as its partial inverse by [F4]. The tensor product of the inclusions $N_1\otimes N_2\to M_1\otimes M_2$ is injective and $U_i$-linear, and for a vector of $N_1\otimes N_2$ its admissible decomposition computed inside $N_1\otimes N_2$ is also admissible in $M_1\otimes M_2$, so by uniqueness [F5] it is the admissible decomposition there; hence the operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ of $M_1\otimes M_2$ restrict on the image to the string operators computed from $N_1,N_2$. [F2, F4, F5, F6]

2.1 The rank-one computation. Apply [F3] to the pair $(w_1,w_2)$ with divided bases $v_j=F_i^{(j)}w_1$, $w_k=F_i^{(k)}w_2$ and their $A_0$-tensor lattice $\Lambda:=\sum_{j,k}A_0\,v_j\otimes w_k\subseteq L_1\otimes L_2$, which is preserved by both string operators by [F3] and by step 1.2; modulo $q\Lambda$ one has $\tilde f_i(v_{n_1}\otimes w_{n_2})=v_{n_1+1}\otimes w_{n_2}$ if $a_1-n_1>n_2$ and $v_{n_1}\otimes w_{n_2+1}$ otherwise, while $\tilde e_i$ acts on the first factor if $a_1-n_1\ge n_2$ and on the second otherwise, with $0$ outside the divided-basis ranges. [step 1.2, F3]

3.1 Transport to the residues. Since $h\in\Lambda$, step 2.1 computes $\tilde f_ih$ and $\tilde e_ih$ modulo $q\Lambda\subseteq q(L_1\otimes L_2)$, and the residues of $v_{n_1+1}=F_i^{(n_1+1)}w_1$ and $v_{n_1}=F_i^{(n_1)}w_1$ are $\tilde f_ib_1$ and $b_1$; likewise on the second factor by [F2]. Because $a_1-n_1=\varphi_i(b_1)$ by [F6] and $n_2=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, the two cases of step 2.1 are exactly $\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ and $\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ for $\tilde f_i$, and $\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ or $\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ for $\tilde e_i$, giving the displayed two-case rules for the residue $b_1\otimes b_2$ of $h$; a selected factor with $\tilde f_i$ or $\tilde e_i$ equal to $0$ produces the value $0$, consistently on both sides of the congruence. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F6, algebra]

4.1 Stability of the tensor lattice. For arbitrary $u_j\in L_j$ use the full string decomposition of [F2]: $u_j=\sum_nF_i^{(n)}w_{j,n}$ with finitely many nonzero $w_{j,n}\in L_j\cap\ker E_i$, and each pair $(w_{1,n},w_{2,n'})$ spans a finite rank-one block as in step 1.2 whose $A_0$-tensor lattice is preserved by both string operators by [F3]; since the inclusions commute with the operators (step 1.2), every term of the finite expansion of $u_1\otimes u_2$ has its images under $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ inside $L_1\otimes L_2$, and linearity gives $\tilde e_i(L_1\otimes L_2)\subseteq L_1\otimes L_2$ and $\tilde f_i(L_1\otimes L_2)\subseteq L_1\otimes L_2$. In particular $\tilde f_i(q(L_1\otimes L_2))\subseteq q(L_1\otimes L_2)$ and likewise for $\tilde e_i$, so the congruence $u_1\otimes u_2\equiv h$ of step 1.1 may be transported by the operators and the two-case rules of step 3.1 hold for the residues of arbitrary lifts, not only for $h$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, F3, F7]

5.1 Operator rules and residues. Combining steps 3.1 and 4.1: for all $b_1\in B_1,b_2\in B_2$ the classes $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)$ and $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2)$ are computed by the displayed two-case rules, and they lie in $(B_1\otimes B_2)\cup\{0\}$ because each case is the residue of an element of the form $v\otimes w$ with $v\in B_1\cup\{0\}$, $w\in B_2\cup\{0\}$; the equality case $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ sends $\tilde f_i$ to the second factor, since the first case requires the strict inequality, and $\tilde e_i$ to the first factor, since its first case is non-strict. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F2, F6]

6.1 Partial inverses. Suppose first $\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ and let $b':=\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2\ne0$; then $\varphi_i(\tilde f_ib_1)=\varphi_i(b_1)-1\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ by [F6], so the $\tilde e_i$-rule of step 5.1 selects the first factor at $b'$ and $\tilde e_ib'=\tilde e_i\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2=b_1\otimes b_2$ by the factor partial inverse [F1]. Suppose next $\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ and $b':=b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2\ne0$; then $\tilde f_ib_2\ne0$ and $\varepsilon_i(\tilde f_ib_2)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)+1>\varphi_i(b_1)$ by [F6], so the $\tilde e_i$-rule selects the second factor and $\tilde e_ib'=b_1\otimes\tilde e_i\tilde f_ib_2=b_1\otimes b_2$. The converse implication is the same computation read backwards, and at the tie $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ both consistency conditions hold simultaneously: this is exactly why $\tilde e_i$ is assigned the non-strict and $\tilde f_i$ the strict comparison. [step 5.1, F1, F6]

7.1 Conclusion. By [F7] the pair $(L_1\otimes L_2,B_1\otimes B_2)$ has the lattice axioms of generation over $\mathbb Q(q)$, weight grading and residue-basis properties; step 4.1 supplies operator stability and step 5.1 the operator axioms on $B_1\otimes B_2$; step 6.1 supplies the partial-inverse axiom. Hence it is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$ whose crystal is the tensor product crystal $B_1\otimes B_2$ of [F8] with the displayed rules. Every step used finite string data of two vectors and the one-factor crystal bases; no finite dimensionality, bounded support, uniform nilpotence or choice principle is assumed. [step 5.1, step 6.1, F7, F8, F9, given] ∎

items.title: The dual crystal: reversed arrows, negated weights and swapped $\varepsilon/\varphi$
items.statement:
Let $B$ be the crystal of a crystal basis $(L,B)$ of an integrable module ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]], [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]); its operators are the partial maps $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i:B\to B\cup\{0\}$ satisfying $\tilde e_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde f_ib'$, and $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ satisfy $\varphi_i(b)-\varepsilon_i(b)=\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$.

Define the **dual crystal** $B^\vee:=\{b^\vee:b\in B\}$ by
$$wt(b^\vee):=-wt(b),\qquad \varepsilon_i(b^\vee):=\varphi_i(b),\qquad \varphi_i(b^\vee):=\varepsilon_i(b),\qquad \tilde f_i(b^\vee):=(\tilde e_ib)^\vee,\qquad \tilde e_i(b^\vee):=(\tilde f_ib)^\vee,$$
with $0^\vee:=0$. Then:

(i) $B^\vee$ satisfies the crystal axioms: $(\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i)$ are partial inverses, the arrows of $B^\vee$ are the arrows of $B$ with orientation reversed, the displayed $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are exactly the maximal iterated powers, and $(B^\vee)^\vee=B$ canonically;

(ii) **tensor products reverse order.** For crystals $B_1,B_2$ as above the map $b_1\otimes b_2\mapsto b_2^\vee\otimes b_1^\vee$ is an isomorphism of crystals $(B_1\otimes B_2)^\vee\to B_2^\vee\otimes B_1^\vee$ for the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]].

The construction is stated for crystals of crystal bases of integrable modules, where $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are finite and nonnegative. For the negative-half crystal of [[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]] only the formal $\varphi_i=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,wt\rangle$, which may be negative, is defined, and no dual is asserted there. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
Reverse e/f, negate weights and exchange maximal string lengths; two duals restore all data. For the tensor swap S, source dual lowering is original raising, with p>=s or pp. Source dual raising is original lowering, with p>s or p<=s, matching target raising at s

=p. Thus S intertwines both operators, weights and string lengths, including zero endpoints. Infinite negative-half strings are excluded; no choice is used.

items.title: Uniqueness: crystal bases of integrable modules decompose into highest weight crystals
items.statement:
**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).

(i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.

(ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.

(iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

**Choice.** The axiom of choice is declared in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used to obtain the decomposition of $M$ into simple integrable highest weight modules from [[prop-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-modules-are-semisimple]], which selects a maximal independent family of simple submodules simultaneously. It also permits simultaneous choices of lifts of the finite residue bases in the possibly infinite family of top spaces. After those choices, each lattice and crystal argument is finite and choice-free. No incompatible-axiom branch is used, and no global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness is assumed. The index set $J$ need not be finite in affine or indefinite type; local weight finiteness means only finitely many summands contribute to any fixed label-weight space.
items.strategy: Under the declared AC semisimplicity decomposition, isolate a maximal top isotypic part. Finite residue lifts give its standard top basis. Standard lowering generators give a full lattice, and minimal-pole descent proves equality with L intersect N0. Height induction splits lattice projections. For a residue vertex with nonzero N0 component, raise to its known N0 basis and use partial inversion to return it to that basis, proving residue splitting. The finite-level depth D(nu)=max_a ht(lambda_a-nu) orders constituent tops; only finitely many contribute to a fixed label. AC also supplies simultaneous top-residue lifts. Resulting algebraic direct sums may be infinite but are locally weight-finite.

items.title: Highest weight components in a tensor product crystal
items.statement:
**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited through [[thm-crystal-bases-of-integrable-modules-decompose-into-highest-weight-crystals]]. Let $M_1,M_2$ be integrable chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules with finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight sets contained in finite unions of cones, let $(L_1,B_1),(L_2,B_2)$ be crystal bases of $M_1,M_2$, and let $B_1\otimes B_2$ be the crystal of $M_1\otimes M_2$ ([[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]], [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]]).

(a) **Highest vertices.** For $b=b_1\otimes b_2\in B_1\otimes B_2$ the following are equivalent: (i) $b$ is a highest weight element, i.e. $\tilde e_ib=0$ for every $i\in I$; (ii) $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle$ for every $i\in I$; (iii) $\varepsilon_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=0$ for every $i\in I$. In this case $wt(b)=wt(b_1)+wt(b_2)$ is dominant.

(b) **Generated components.** For every highest vertex $b\in B_1\otimes B_2$ of weight $\lambda$, the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ is a connected component of $B_1\otimes B_2$, is isomorphic as a crystal to the canonical $B(\lambda)=\mathcal B(\lambda)$ of [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]], and $\lambda\in P^+$.

(c) **Decomposition.** $B_1\otimes B_2$ is the disjoint union of the subcrystals $F(b)$ over the highest weight elements $b\in B_1\otimes B_2$, each of which is a highest weight crystal in the sense of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]; the multiplicity of $B(\lambda)$ as a component equals the multiplicity of $V(\lambda)$ in the tensor product module $M_1\otimes M_2$.

No choice principle beyond the inherited one is used.
items.strategy:
(a) By [[lem-crystal-tensor-product-weight-epsilon-and-phi-formulas]](b), $\varepsilon_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\max(\varepsilon_i(b_1),\varepsilon_i(b_2)-\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle)$, so $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=0$ for all $i$ if and only if this maximum is $0$ for all $i$, i.e. $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle$; this is the equivalence of (i),(ii) and, by definition, of (iii). Dominance: $\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle=\varphi_i(b)\ge0$ because $\varepsilon_i(b)=0$ and $\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$ is finite and nonnegative for a crystal of an integrable module ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]).

(b) Apply [[thm-crystal-bases-of-integrable-modules-decompose-into-highest-weight-crystals]] to $M_1\otimes M_2$, which satisfies the category hypotheses by [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]](a)-(c), with the crystal basis $(L_1\otimes L_2,B_1\otimes B_2)$ of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. The theorem decomposes the crystal into components $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ whose highest vertices are exactly the highest weight elements (clause (iii)). The component of $b$ therefore is a highest weight crystal of weight $\lambda=wt(b)$; by [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]](ii) its vertex set is $F(b)$, and its identification with $\mathcal B(\lambda)$ is the transported isomorphism of the uniqueness theorem.

(c) The disjoint-union statement is the component decomposition of the same theorem together with the uniqueness of the highest vertex in each component; the multiplicity statement is clause (ii) there applied to $M_1\otimes M_2$, whose highest weight multiplicities are those of the tensor product module. The axiom of choice is used only through the uniqueness theorem, where it is already declared; no new nonconstructive step occurs.

title: Tensor-Product Crystals and Highest-Weight Crystal Uniqueness — Examples

items.title: Changing the equality case in the tensor rule breaks the partial-inverse axiom
items.statement:
Claim refuted: on the product of two crystals one may exchange the two equality cases while retaining the comparison direction, namely

$$\tilde f_i^{\prime}(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2\ \text{ if }\ \varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2),\qquad \tilde e_i^{\prime}(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2\ \text{ if }\ \varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2),$$

with the second factor used in the remaining cases and $0$ whenever the selected factor maps to $0$; that is, the two equality cases of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] are exchanged.

Counterexample: take $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, the rank-one simples of highest weights $a=b=2$ with divided bases $v_j=F_1^{(j)}v_0,\ w_k=F_1^{(k)}w_0$, and the vertex $b=v_1\otimes w_1$. Then $\varphi_1(v_1)=1=\varepsilon_1(w_1)$, so the modified rule uses the non-strict comparison and acts on the first factor: $\tilde f_1^{\prime}(v_1\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_1$. At the image $b'=v_2\otimes w_1$ one has $\varphi_1(v_2)=0\le\varepsilon_1(w_1)=1$, and the modified $\tilde e_1^{\prime}$ acts on the first factor only when $\varphi_1>\varepsilon_1$, so it acts on the second factor: $\tilde e_1^{\prime}(v_2\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_0\ne v_1\otimes w_1$. Hence $\tilde f_1^{\prime}b=b'$ while $\tilde e_1^{\prime}b'\ne b$: the partial-inverse axiom fails, so $(B(a)\otimes B(b),\tilde e^{\prime},\tilde f^{\prime})$ is not a crystal, and a fortiori not the crystal $B(a)\otimes B(b)$ of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. The same failure occurs if one uses the strict comparison for both operators, or the non-strict comparison for both; by contrast the rank-one computation of [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]] shows that with the convention of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] the string through $v_0\otimes w_1$ is $v_0\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_2$ of length three, whereas the modified rule produces the four-element chain $v_0\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_1,v_2\otimes w_1,v_2\otimes w_2$, so the modified rule has the wrong lowering-chain length and cannot be the crystal of $V(2)\otimes V(2)=V(4)\oplus V(2)\oplus V(0)$.
items.strategy: At a=b=2, the exchanged-equality rule takes (1,1) under f prime to (2,1), whose e prime image is (2,0), so inversion fails. Strict-both fails at (0,1), and non-strict-both at (1,1). The proper chain through (0,1) has three positions; exchanged equality has four. Malformed lowering chains are distinguished from crystal components. All computations are finite and choice-free.

items.title: The tensor crystal $B(1)\otimes B(1)$ for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, $I=\{1\}$, with fundamental weight $\lambda_1$ and simple root $\alpha_1=2\lambda_1$. Let $V(1)$ be the two-dimensional simple integrable module with highest vector $v_0$ and crystal $B(1)=\{v_0,v_1\}$, where $v_1=F_1v_0$; the $i$-string is $v_0\xrightarrow{1}v_1$ with $wt(v_0)=\lambda_1$, $wt(v_1)=-\lambda_1$ and $\varepsilon_1(v_0)=0,\ \varphi_1(v_0)=1,\ \varepsilon_1(v_1)=1,\ \varphi_1(v_1)=0$ (JKK Example 5.1(a) with $m=1$).

Compute the tensor crystal $B(1)\otimes B(1)$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] with the two-case rule of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. Writing the four vertices as $v_j\otimes v_k$ with $j,k\in\{0,1\}$, the rule gives

$$\tilde f_1(v_j\otimes v_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j+1}\otimes v_k,&1-j>k,\\ v_j\otimes v_{k+1},&1-j\le k,\end{cases}\qquad \tilde e_1(v_j\otimes v_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j-1}\otimes v_k,&1-j\ge k,\\ v_j\otimes v_{k-1},&1-j<k.\end{cases}$$

Consequently: $v_0\otimes v_0$ is the unique highest vertex of weight $2\lambda_1$ and generates the chain $v_0\otimes v_0\to v_1\otimes v_0\to v_1\otimes v_1$; the remaining vertex $v_0\otimes v_1$ has weight $0$, is killed by $\tilde e_1$ and by $\tilde f_1$, and forms a one-element component; and $\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1$ of the four vertices are $(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(0,0)$ at $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ respectively. Hence $B(1)\otimes B(1)=B(2)\sqcup B(0)$, matching the classical decomposition $V(1)\otimes V(1)=V(2)\oplus V(0)$ of dimensions $4=3+1$; here $B(2)$ is the three-element $1$-chain of weights $2\lambda_1,0,-2\lambda_1$ and $B(0)$ the one-element crystal of weight $0$.
items.strategy: Enumerate four vertices: 00->10->11 is a three-element chain and 01 is isolated; the max formulas give all epsilon/phi values. Match these one-color chains to B(2) and B(0). In the module tensor square, t=00 generates V(2), s=01-q_1 10 generates the trivial line, and determinant 1+q_1^2 is nonzero. Thus 4=3+1. The calculation is choice-free.

items.title: Highest components in the $A_2$ tensor crystal $B(\lambda_1)\otimes B(\lambda_1)$
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3$ with simple roots $\alpha_1=2\lambda_1-\lambda_2$, $\alpha_2=-\lambda_1+2\lambda_2$ and $\langle h_i,\lambda_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$. The three-dimensional simple module $V(\lambda_1)$ has crystal $B(\lambda_1)=\{u_1,u_2,u_3\}$ with weights $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2-\lambda_1,\ -\lambda_2$ and arrows $u_1\xrightarrow{1}u_2\xrightarrow{2}u_3$; its only nonzero $\varepsilon$-values are $\varepsilon_1(u_2)=1,\ \varepsilon_2(u_3)=1$, and $\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$.

In the tensor crystal $B(\lambda_1)\otimes B(\lambda_1)$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] the criterion of [[thm-highest-weight-components-in-a-tensor-product-crystal]](a) applies. A vertex $b_1\otimes b_2$ is highest exactly when $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ for $i=1,2$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle$ for $i=1,2$. Since $\varepsilon_1(u_2)=1$ and $\varepsilon_2(u_3)=1$, only $b_1=u_1$ can occur, so the highest vertices are
$$u_1\otimes u_1\quad(\text{weight }2\lambda_1),\qquad u_1\otimes u_2\quad(\text{weight }\lambda_2),$$
the second because $\varepsilon_1(u_2)=1\le\langle h_1,wt(u_1)\rangle=1$ and $\varepsilon_2(u_2)=0\le\langle h_2,wt(u_1)\rangle=0$, while $u_1\otimes u_3$ fails since $\varepsilon_2(u_3)=1>\langle h_2,wt(u_1)\rangle=0$. By [[thm-highest-weight-components-in-a-tensor-product-crystal]](b) the two generated components are the highest weight crystals $B(2\lambda_1)$ and $B(\lambda_2)$, so the nine vertices split as $B(\lambda_1)\otimes B(\lambda_1)=B(2\lambda_1)\sqcup B(\lambda_2)$, matching $V(\lambda_1)\otimes V(\lambda_1)=V(2\lambda_1)\oplus V(\lambda_2)$ with dimensions $9=6+3$.
items.strategy: Construct the standard three-vector module and verify toral, mixed and A2 Serre relations. Universality and its explicit lowering words identify the canonical lattice and crystal. The highest-vertex criterion gives 11 and 12, of weights 2lambda1 and lambda2. Enumerate all nine vertices and eight lowering arrows with raising inverses, obtaining components of six and three vertices. The component/multiplicity theorem identifies canonical crystals and module constituents under its inherited AC. Classical symmetric and alternating tensors have the same dimensions via (1+-flip)/2.

items.title: Dual crystals reverse arrows and weights: two small computations
items.statement:
The example computes the dual crystal of [[prop-dual-crystal-and-reversal-conventions]] in two small cases.

(A) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, let $B(1)=\{v_0\xrightarrow{1}v_1\}$ with $wt(v_0)=\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1)=-\lambda_1$ and $\varepsilon_1(v_0)=0,\varphi_1(v_0)=1,\varepsilon_1(v_1)=1,\varphi_1(v_1)=0$ (as in [[ex-tensor-crystal-b-one-tensor-b-one-for-sl-two]]). Then $B(1)^\vee=\{v_0^\vee,v_1^\vee\}$ has the single arrow $v_1^\vee\xrightarrow{1}v_0^\vee$, weights $wt(v_0^\vee)=-\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1^\vee)=\lambda_1$, and $(\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1)$ equal to $(1,0)$ at $v_0^\vee$ and $(0,1)$ at $v_1^\vee$. Hence $B(1)^\vee\cong B(1)$ as crystals, realized with the highest vertex $v_1^\vee$.

(B) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3$, let $B(\lambda_1)=\{u_1\xrightarrow{1}u_2\xrightarrow{2}u_3\}$ be the standard crystal of [[ex-highest-components-in-a-small-type-a-two-tensor-crystal]]. Then $B(\lambda_1)^\vee=\{u_1^\vee,u_2^\vee,u_3^\vee\}$ has the arrows $u_2^\vee\xrightarrow{1}u_1^\vee$ and $u_3^\vee\xrightarrow{2}u_2^\vee$, weights $-\lambda_1,\ -\lambda_2+\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2$ at $u_1^\vee,u_2^\vee,u_3^\vee$, and $\varepsilon/\varphi$ exchanged; this is the crystal $B(\lambda_2)$ of the dual three-dimensional module, so $B(\lambda_1)^\vee\cong B(\lambda_2)$.

(C) On the tensor square of (A), $(B(1)\otimes B(1))^\vee\cong B(1)^\vee\otimes B(1)^\vee$ under $(b_1\otimes b_2)^\vee\mapsto b_2^\vee\otimes b_1^\vee$; both sides split as $B(2)\sqcup B(0)$ because each of $B(2),B(0)$ is self-dual along the chain reversal (weights $2\lambda_1,0,-2\lambda_1$ are symmetric).

Check the A2 three-vector module relations explicitly, identify V(lambda2) by the direct highest-weight universality theorem, and compute its canonical lowering-word lattice. Antipode formulas and an explicit dual-basis rescaling identify it as the contragredient standard module. Compute the order-reversing tensor swap, including the isolated tie vertex.
